design_detail: Prospective observational study of symptom course during monitored inpatient abstinence. 56 adults with methamphetamine dependence, not seeking treatment, were admitted to a research ward (UCLA General Clinical Research Center) for neuroimaging studies lasting 2 or 5 weeks and rated daily on a 30-item rater-scored Methamphetamine Withdrawal Questionnaire (MAWQ) and weekly on the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), Brief Symptom Inventory (BSI) and a visual analogue scale (VAS) for craving; 89 healthy outpatient controls completed the BDI and BSI weekly. Analyses used subsets of 25–32 participants with methamphetamine dependence; linear mixed-effects models for time, ANCOVA with Bonferroni correction for group comparisons, Pearson correlations for craving and depression.
can_establish: How self-reported depressive and general psychiatric symptoms and craving changed over 2–5 weeks of monitored inpatient abstinence in 25–32 non-treatment-seeking people with methamphetamine dependence and no other current psychiatric diagnosis, relative to healthy outpatients.
cannot_establish: The course of withdrawal in people who seek treatment, have psychiatric comorbidity or stay in their usual surroundings; whether the changes reflect abstinence rather than hospitalization, decline from a peak at admission, or repeated testing (no inpatient comparison group); how often psychosis occurs in withdrawal (only symptom-distress subscales and three questionnaire items were used); or when relapse risk is highest (relapse was not measured).

sample.recruitment: Advertisement (print, radio, internet) for paid research participation; participants with methamphetamine dependence were not seeking treatment and were studied as inpatients in a series of neuroimaging studies; controls were studied as outpatients (Methods › Participants; In-patient milieu).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Methamphetamine group: DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence, active use with a positive urine screen at entry, self-reported use within 7 days before admission, no dependence on other substances except nicotine. Controls: no history of substance use disorder except nicotine dependence, negative urine tests throughout. Both: no major medical illness including HIV seropositivity, no other current Axis I diagnosis on the SCID-IV, no recent psychotropic medication; light alcohol use (described as equivalent to 7.5 drinks a week) allowed. Participants whose self-reported last use disagreed with urine toxicology were excluded from analysis (number not given) (Methods › Participants; MAWQ section).
sample.demographics: Controls vs methamphetamine group: age 31.7 (SD 8.3) vs 33.8 (8.2); men 50.6% vs 62.5%; years of education 14.8 (2.1) vs 12.6 (1.3); maternal education 14.4 (2.7) vs 12.7 (2.7); married 20.2% vs 5.4%; unemployed 25.8% vs 80.3%; on parole or probation 0% vs 21.4%; cigarette smokers 44.9% vs 91.1%; white 66.3% vs 53.6%, Hispanic 5.6% vs 26.8%, Black 12.4% vs 1.8%, Asian 10.1% vs 3.6% (Table 1).
sample.attrition: Of 56 enrolled, the analyses include 32 (MAWQ, days 1–14), 28 (BDI), 26 (craving VAS and craving–BDI correlations) and 25 (BSI); BSI controls n=85 of 89. Studies lasted 2 or 5 weeks, so weeks 3–5 come from a further unreported subset; the number assessed at each week is not given. The authors state the analysed subsets did not differ demographically from the whole group (data not shown) (Results › Demographics; Table 2; figure legends).
sample.selection_effects: Non-treatment-seeking, paid volunteers for imaging research, with other current psychiatric disorders excluded: people most likely to have persisting depression or psychosis were screened out, which biases towards fast resolution; the authors note treatment-seeking people may have more severe or longer symptoms (Limitations). Analysed subsets (25–32 of 56) were not shown to be comparable with the full sample. Inpatients were compared with outpatient controls.

exposure.measurement: SCID-IV diagnosis of methamphetamine dependence; recent use confirmed by positive urine screen at entry; abstinence on the ward confirmed by daily urine and breath-alcohol tests; days since last use from self-report corroborated by entry toxicology (urine kit detection window typically 48–72 hours, per the manufacturer) (Methods).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Mean 11.1 (SD 7.2) years of methamphetamine use and 20.4 (SD 8.6) days of use in the past 30 days (Table 1); most named smoking as their main route (In-patient milieu). Amounts not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Dependence on other substances except nicotine excluded; light alcohol use allowed; 91.1% smoked tobacco and smoking was allowed freely on the ward to avoid nicotine withdrawal. Craving for alcohol, opioids and cocaine was measured by VAS but not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Study entry is defined as days 0–1 of abstinence in the Figure 3 legend, although participants could have last used up to 7 days before admission; weekly assessments are described both as weeks of abstinence and as weeks of hospitalization. Abstinence was verified daily on the ward.

comparison.controls: 89 healthy outpatients without substance use disorder (other than nicotine dependence), recruited by the same advertisements, assessed weekly with BDI and BSI only.
comparison.matching: Described as matched; groups did not differ in age or sex but differed in education, maternal education, ethnicity, marital status, employment, parole or probation and smoking (Table 1). BSI comparisons adjusted for ethnicity, education, maternal education and smoking; BDI comparisons for demographic and behavioural variables that differed (Methods › Data analysis; Results).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measurement before methamphetamine use; premorbid depression, childhood adversity and family history not reported. Unemployment and parole or probation status, which differed sharply, were not among the listed covariates.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: No substance use disorder other than nicotine; negative urine tests throughout; 44.9% smoked tobacco.

outcomes.instruments: MAWQ: 30 items plus vital signs, rater-scored on a four-point scale, adapted from the Amphetamine Withdrawal Questionnaire by one of the authors and expanded with symptoms seen anecdotally in clinical practice (joint pain, red or itchy eyes, headache, anger), given daily at about 9 a.m.; BDI and BSI (11 subscales) weekly in both groups; VAS craving weekly in the methamphetamine group (Methods).
outcomes.validity_norms: No validation data are reported for the adapted MAWQ, and the authors found it gave lower symptom intensities than the self-report scales (Limitations). BDI entry scores are interpreted against treatment-seeking psychiatric outpatients and BSI entry scores against general adult psychiatric outpatients. The BSI psychoticism and paranoid-ideation subscales are self-report distress scales, not diagnostic measures of psychosis.
outcomes.operationalization: Withdrawal was operationalized as MAWQ item endorsement and change over days 1–14; depression as BDI score; psychopathology including psychotic symptoms as BSI subscale scores; craving as VAS score. No severity thresholds or definitions of resolution are given; resolved is used to mean a decline to stable low levels or to the control level.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Partial: group comparisons used Bonferroni-corrected post hoc tests; the 33 MAWQ rows (30 items, 3 vital signs) were each tested at P<0.05 without correction (about 1.7 false positives expected; a Bonferroni threshold would be about 0.0015); the five craving–BDI correlations were uncorrected.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable for self-report scales; MAWQ raters knew participants' group and day of abstinence.

analysis.effect_sizes: None reported: P values only, and BDI, BSI and craving values are shown only in figures (images, not extracted). Editors' calculations: entry prevalence on the MAWQ (n=32, Wilson 95% CI): thinking often about methamphetamine 72% (55–84), craving 69% (51–82), increased appetite 63% (45–77), tiredness or low energy 56% (39–72), depressed 25% (13–42), sleep difficulties 22% (11–39), feeling watched or talked about 9% (3–24), suicidal thoughts 6% (2–20), hearing voices 3% (0.6–16), feeling touched 3% (0.6–16). Education difference between groups from Table 1 means and SDs: standardized difference about 1.2 (t about 7.0), not the printed F 4.4, P 0.04.
analysis.covariates: Group comparisons adjusted for ethnicity, education, maternal education and cigarette smoking (BSI), and for demographic and behavioural variables that differed (BDI); within-group time effects unadjusted.
analysis.selective_reporting: Craving for alcohol, opioids and cocaine was measured but not reported; control-group BDI time course and analysed-subset demographics are described as not shown; n at each weekly time point not reported; correlation coefficients appear only in Figure 3.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 25–32 participants per analysis, and fewer after week 2, a non-significant difference from controls at week 4 (P=0.07) cannot be read as equivalence.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 28 participants, BDI scores averaging about 12 at entry fell over the first 2 weeks to stable low levels but stayed above controls' scores for the first 3 weeks and only approached them at week 4 (P=0.07). BSI subscale scores, including psychoticism and paranoid ideation, were raised at entry and fell to a low baseline by the end of week 2 (n=25). VAS craving stayed high through week 1, fell after 2 weeks and persisted at a lower level to week 5 (n=26). On the rater-scored MAWQ, craving and depressed mood items did not change significantly over 14 days; 3 of 32 endorsed feeling watched or talked about and 1 of 32 hearing voices at entry.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes: "Depressive and psychotic symptoms accompany acute withdrawal from methamphetamine but resolve within 1 week." The Results show depressive symptoms above controls for 3 weeks, and the Discussion itself speaks of a reduction within 2 weeks and of withdrawal symptoms resolving within 14 days. The abstract calls psychotic symptoms prevalent, but no prevalence of psychotic symptoms is reported beyond 1–3 of 32 item endorsements and raised BSI subscale means. The Discussion says the correlation data, with the literature, give strong evidence that days 7–14 are the most vulnerable time for relapse, although relapse could not occur or be measured on a locked research ward, the correlation rests on 26 people at two uncorrected time points, and symptoms at entry may partly reflect the end of a period of use and sleep loss rather than withdrawal. Withdrawal is described as mild and well tolerated with reference to Table 2, which reports only how many endorsed each item, not severity.

timeline.event: Newton et al.: 19 non-treatment-seeking people with methamphetamine dependence; generally mild depressive symptoms that varied widely and resolved within 2 weeks of abstinence (as described in this paper's Introduction)

McGregor et al.: 21 treatment-seeking people followed 3 weeks; acute phase of 7–10 days peaking about 24 hours after last use, then a milder subacute phase for about 2 more weeks (as described in this paper's Introduction)
Simon et al.: neuropsychological change during early abstinence, one of the same UCLA inpatient research programme's reports that this paper lists as based on its participants (refs 22–29)
This study: depressive and psychiatric symptoms fall over 1–2 weeks of inpatient abstinence; craving persists at a lower level to 5 weeks

replication.where_it_stands: Three small studies (19, 21 and 25–32 analysed participants) agree that depressive symptoms are highest at the start of abstinence and fall over the first 1–3 weeks, and that craving outlasts them; none followed treatment-seeking people with psychiatric comorbidity in their usual environment, and none measured relapse.

funding.funder: NIH grants P20 DA022539, R01 DA020726, R01 DA15179 (Edythe D. London) and M01 RR 00865 (UCLA General Clinical Research Center) (Acknowledgments).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychiatry and Biobehavioral Sciences, Brain Research Institute, and Department of Molecular and Medical Pharmacology, University of California at Los Angeles. The MAWQ was adapted by one of the authors (Richard Rawson). Read as the PMC author manuscript of Addiction 2010;105:1809–1818.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study of treatment-seeking and community samples, including people with psychiatric comorbidity, with toxicology-verified time since last use, a validated withdrawal scale and structured interviews for depression and psychosis assessed daily in the first week and weekly to 3 months, a design that separates abstinence from hospitalization and repeated-testing effects (an inpatient comparison group or outpatient follow-up), and relapse recorded after discharge.

domains.note: For the comparison with controls: large differences in education (standardized difference about 1.2), employment, parole or probation and smoking, only partly adjusted; inpatient versus outpatient setting. For the time course: no comparison group for hospitalization, regression from a peak at admission or repeated testing.

Dependence by SCID and abstinence verified daily, but time since last use at entry is self-reported and the entry time point is defined inconsistently (days 0–1 of abstinence versus last use up to 7 days earlier).
Paid non-treatment-seeking imaging volunteers with other current psychiatric disorders excluded; analyses on unexplained subsets of 25–32 of 56.
Cue-free, monitored ward with individual housing and medication for physical complaints only; neuroimaging procedures. Symptom and craving trajectories may differ outside such a setting.
Up to 31 of 56 participants missing from each analysis; numbers at weeks 3–5 unreported; exclusions for discrepant self-report not counted.

Validated self-report scales, but unblinded repeated administration; the adapted MAWQ has no reported validation and disagreed with self-report; psychosis measured only by symptom-distress subscales and single items.
Many outcomes (46 measures) with figures only; craving for other drugs and control-group BDI course not reported; abstract emphasizes resolution within 1 week.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The direction of the within-group change (symptoms highest at admission and falling over 1–2 weeks) is plausible and agrees with two earlier small studies, but its timing and size cannot be separated from hospitalization, regression from an admission peak and repeated testing, the sample was selected to exclude psychiatric comorbidity, and about half the participants are missing from each analysis. Comparisons with controls are confounded by setting and sociodemographic differences.

key_findings.finding: Sample: 56 people with methamphetamine dependence (mean 11.1 years of use, 20.4 days of use in the past 30; 91.1% tobacco smokers; 80.3% unemployed) and 89 healthy controls; groups similar in age (33.8 vs 31.7) and sex (62.5% vs 50.6% men) but different in education (12.6 vs 14.8 years), ethnicity, employment, parole or probation and smoking.

At entry (n=32) the most frequent MAWQ symptoms were thinking often about methamphetamine (23, 72%), craving (22, 68%), increased appetite (20, 63%), tiredness or low energy (18, 56%), restlessness (13, 40%), lack of motivation (12, 38%) and anxiety (11, 34%); depressed mood 8 (25%); suicidal thoughts 2 (6%).

Over days 1–14 of abstinence, MAWQ items with a significant time effect were red or itchy eyes (F 4.33, P<0.001), tiredness or low energy (F 5.36, P<0.001), increased appetite (F 3.23, P<0.001), sleep difficulties (F 3.16, P<0.001), lack of motivation (F 2.8, P=0.001), reduced sexual pleasure (F 2.22, P=0.008), feeling watched or talked about (F 2.19, P=0.009) and thinking often about methamphetamine (F 2.04, P=0.02); the craving item (P=0.79) and depressed item (P=0.26) did not change significantly. Vital signs did not change.
key_findings.note: 33 rows tested at P<0.05 without correction; degrees of freedom not given. The authors say substantial changes occurred only within the first 14 days.

key_findings.finding: Psychotic-type items at entry on the rater-scored MAWQ: feeling watched or talked about 3 of 32 (9%), feeling touched when no one is there 1 of 32 (3%), hearing voices 1 of 32 (3%).

BDI (n=28 vs 89 controls): mean about 12 at entry (mild–moderate range), decreasing over the first 2 weeks to stable low levels (time effect P<0.001); still significantly higher than controls during the first 3 weeks after adjustment (P<0.05); approaching control levels only at the end of week 4 (P=0.07).
key_findings.note: Weekly means appear only in Figure 1 (image, not extracted).

key_findings.finding: BSI (n=25 vs 85 controls): most subscales except phobia were raised at entry, fell significantly during week 1 and reached a low baseline by the end of week 2 (P<0.004); time effects included psychoticism P=0.003 and paranoid ideation P=0.003; by week 2 all subscales except additional symptoms were at the control level, although the same paragraph says the methamphetamine group scored higher than controls at most time points.
key_findings.locator: Results › Psychiatric symptoms; Figure 4 legend (panels A–K)

key_findings.finding: Craving VAS (n=26): high at entry and through week 1, significantly lower after more than 2 weeks of abstinence (P<0.01 vs entry), and still present at a reduced level through week 5.
key_findings.locator: Results › Craving for MA; Figure 2 legend
key_findings.note: The number of participants assessed in weeks 3–5 (5-week studies only) is not reported.

key_findings.finding: Craving and BDI were not correlated at entry (P=0.29) but were at the end of week 1 (P=0.004) and week 2 (P=0.03), and not at weeks 3 (P=0.8) or 4 (P=0.09); n=26.
key_findings.locator: Results › Craving for MA and depressive symptoms; Figure 3 legend
key_findings.note: Correlation coefficients are printed only inside Figure 3 (image, not extracted); five uncorrected tests.

key_findings.finding: Ward conditions: individual housing, cues and media restricted, daily urine and breath tests, questionnaires daily at about 9 a.m., medication only for physical symptoms (none for insomnia, anxiety or fatigue), free tobacco smoking, concurrent MRI and PET studies.

The authors list as limitations the small, non-treatment-seeking sample, inpatient cases versus outpatient controls, follow-up of no more than 5 weeks, and lower symptom ratings on the rater-scored MAWQ than on self-report.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints education as 14.8 (SD 2.1) vs 12.6 (SD 1.3) years with F 4.4, P 0.04; those means and SDs give t about 7.0 (F about 49, P below 0.0001; standardized difference about 1.2) with the full groups, so the printed test understates the difference by far (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Education differed much more than the paper suggests; it was a covariate, but residual confounding in comparisons with controls is more likely.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 smoking: 44.9% (40/89) vs 91.1% (51/56) gives a chi-square of about 31 (29 with continuity correction), not the printed 13.2 (editors' calculation); the F tests have error df of 111, 107 and 105, implying about 113, 109 and 107 participants rather than 145, with the missing demographic data not reported; age F 2.4 on 1 and 111 df gives P≈0.12, not 0.15.
reporting_issues.consequence: Conclusions about group differences unchanged, but the table's statistics cannot be reproduced and demographic data were incomplete.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says depressive and psychotic symptoms resolve within 1 week; the Results report BDI scores above controls for 3 weeks and approaching controls only at week 4, and the Discussion describes resolution within 2 weeks (BDI) and 14 days (withdrawal symptoms).
reporting_issues.consequence: The encyclopedia should not cite this paper for one-week resolution of depressive symptoms.

reporting_issues.issue: In the BSI paragraph, all subscales are said to reach the control level by the end of week 2 (except additional symptoms), but the same paragraph says the methamphetamine group scored higher than controls at most time points.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which BSI comparisons remained significant after week 2 cannot be determined from the text; the figure (image) was not extracted.

reporting_issues.issue: Study entry is defined as days 0–1 of abstinence (Figure 3 legend), yet participants could have used up to 7 days before admission, time since last use was used to align participants, and BSI time points are described as weeks of hospitalization (Figure 4 legend).
reporting_issues.consequence: The time axis (days since last use or days since admission) is ambiguous, which matters for any statement about how many days after stopping symptoms resolve.

reporting_issues.issue: Analyses use 25–32 of the 56 participants, and the number assessed at weeks 3–5 is never given; the abstract reports the full 56 without saying this.
reporting_issues.consequence: Late time points, including craving at week 5, rest on an unknown and probably small number of people.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1 gives the BDI range as 0–69 without naming the BDI version; the cited reference compares BDI-IA and BDI-II, which (editors' note) have 21 items scored 0–3, a maximum of 63.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the version used should be confirmed before comparing scores with norms.

reporting_issues.issue: Figures 1–4 are images; the weekly means, standard deviations and correlation coefficients were not extracted (the images could not be rendered without bringing the browser tab to the front).
reporting_issues.consequence: Magnitudes of change and of the craving–depression correlations are not on this card.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC3071736 (NIH author manuscript; all sections, Tables 1–2 as text, Figures 1–4 legends only, acknowledgments, declarations, references; no supplementary material)
